title: 22. Interview: Fault Tolerance
summary: Interview Q&A for Fault Tolerance — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Fault Tolerance interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between fault tolerance and high availability?
**Answer:** Fault tolerance is the ability to continue operating correctly after a component fails — strictly, the user sees no error at all. High availability is a softer goal: the system is up most of the time (e.g., 99.99%), accepting brief periods of degraded or failed service. A fault-tolerant system handles component failure with zero user-visible impact (active-active redundancy, instant failover); a highly available system may have a few seconds of downtime during failover but recovers quickly. The cost difference is enormous: true fault tolerance requires redundant hardware running in lockstep (e.g., Stratus servers, Tandem NonStop), which is expensive. High availability uses commodity hardware with software-managed failover, accepting a small MTTR. In practice, modern distributed systems aim for high availability with very low MTTR (seconds) — close enough to fault-tolerant for most workloads, at a fraction of the cost. The distinction matters when designing for workloads like aerospace or medical devices where even one second of failure is unacceptable — those need true fault tolerance, not just HA.
**Visual:**
```
Fault tolerant:  failure -> user sees nothing  (active-active, lockstep)
High available:  failure -> user sees brief error, then recovery (seconds)
```

### Q2. Explain the heartbeat failure-detection mechanism and its timeout trade-off.
**Answer:** A heartbeat is a periodic "I'm alive" signal sent from a node to a monitor or peers. The monitor expects a heartbeat within a configured interval; if it doesn't arrive within the timeout, the node is suspected dead. The trade-off is fundamental: short timeouts detect failures fast but produce false positives when a node is briefly slow (GC pause, network blip, OS scheduling); long timeouts reduce false positives but extend the window during which a dead node is treated as alive, delaying failover. Production systems tune this carefully: Kubernetes uses 40s node-status timeout (4x the 10s heartbeat interval) to absorb transient slowness. Cassandra uses Phi Accrual failure detection, which tracks the historical heartbeat arrival distribution and outputs a "suspicion level" rather than a binary alive/dead, letting each consumer decide its own threshold. Google Spanner uses adaptive timeouts that learn each region's typical latency. The pitfall: a single global timeout is wrong for heterogeneous clusters — a node in another region needs a longer timeout than a node in the same rack.
**Visual:**
```
heartbeat every 1s | timeout 5s
node:    |H|H|H|H|X|X|X|X|X|X|  -> at 5s of silence, suspect
                                       |
                                       v
                              wait grace (2 more cycles) -> mark dead
```

### Q3. What is a circuit breaker, and how does it prevent cascading failures?
**Answer:** A circuit breaker wraps calls to a downstream service. In its CLOSED state, calls pass through normally. If failures exceed a threshold (e.g., 5 failures in 10 seconds), the breaker opens — it stops calling the downstream and immediately returns an error or fallback. After a recovery interval, it enters HALF_OPEN and allows a single probe call; if the probe succeeds, it closes and resumes traffic; if it fails, it reopens. Without a circuit breaker, a slow downstream causes upstream callers to block waiting for timeouts, exhausting their thread pools and connection pools; this propagates the failure upstream in a cascade. With a circuit breaker, the upstream fails fast, frees its resources, and can continue serving other requests. Netflix Hystrix and resilience4j popularized this in the Java ecosystem. The pitfall: a circuit breaker without a fallback just propagates the failure as an error; you need a real fallback (cached value, default, degraded feature) for the breaker to actually preserve user experience. Also, breakers must be tuned — too sensitive and they trip on normal variance; too lax and they never trip.
**Visual:**
```
CLOSED:    call -> downstream (count failures)
              |
           threshold exceeded
              v
OPEN:      call -> REJECTED immediately (no downstream call)
              |
           recovery timeout
              v
HALF_OPEN: probe call -> success: CLOSE / fail: OPEN
```

### Q4. Explain the bulkhead pattern and why it matters for microservices.
**Answer:** The bulkhead pattern, named after the watertight compartments in a ship's hull, isolates resources so that a failure in one part of the system cannot consume the resources of other parts. In microservices, the typical application is thread pool isolation: instead of one shared thread pool handling all downstream calls, each downstream service gets its own dedicated pool. If downstream A becomes slow, the calls to A pile up in A's pool — but calls to downstream B continue to be served from B's pool, unaffected. Without bulkheads, a single slow downstream exhausts the shared pool and brings down all calls, even to healthy downstreams. Netflix Hystrix implemented this with semaphore- or thread-based isolation per dependency. The trade-off: more pools means more idle threads and slightly higher memory overhead, plus the risk of under-utilization — if A is healthy but B is overloaded, you cannot borrow A's idle threads for B. For most production microservices, the resilience gain outweighs the overhead. The pitfall: bulkheads don't help if the failure mode is shared across bulkheads (e.g., a shared database connection pool underneath), so dependency mapping is essential.
**Visual:**
```
Without bulkhead:                With bulkhead:
  [shared pool: 100 threads]       [pool A: 50]  [pool B: 50]
  A slow -> all 100 blocked        A slow -> only pool A blocked
  B fails too!                     B healthy -> still serving
```

### Q5. How does Google Spanner achieve fault tolerance across datacenters?
**Answer:** Spanner shards data into "tablets," each replicated across at least three datacenters in different regions using Paxos. Writes are committed by a Paxos majority — typically two of three replicas — so a single datacenter failure does not block writes. Each Paxos group has a leader, elected by the replicas; if the leader's datacenter fails, the surviving majority elects a new leader within seconds, and writes resume. Reads can be served from any replica's last-committed value, providing low-latency local reads for non-stale data. Spanner also uses TrueTime, an API that exposes clock uncertainty with bounded error, allowing Spanner to assign globally meaningful commit timestamps and provide external consistency (linearizability across datacenters). The combination — Paxos replication + TrueTime + leader election — gives Spanner fault tolerance that survives the complete failure of one region with no data loss and no consistency violation. The trade-off is latency: every write requires Paxos consensus across regions, adding tens of milliseconds, which Spanner accepts because its target workloads (AdWords, Play, Gmail metadata) value consistency over latency.
**Visual:**
```
Region A: tablet-1 leader         Region B: tablet-1 replica
                                     |
                                     +-- Paxos majority
                                     |
Region C: tablet-1 replica

A fails -> B+C elect new leader -> writes continue, no data loss
```

### Q6. What is chaos engineering, and why is it necessary for proving fault tolerance?
**Answer:** Chaos engineering is the discipline of running controlled failure experiments in production to validate that the system actually behaves fault-tolerantly when components fail. It is necessary because fault tolerance is easy to claim and hard to verify. A team that has designed redundancy, circuit breakers, and failover may believe their system is fault-tolerant, but the only way to know is to actually trigger failures and observe. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances during business hours; Latency Monkey injects network latency; the Simian Army covers a range of failure modes. The result is empirical evidence: either the system continues serving users (proving fault tolerance) or it doesn't (revealing a hidden bug, missing fallback, or stale runbook). The cultural shift is significant — engineers must accept production failures as normal and design accordingly, rather than treating them as exceptional events to be prevented. The pitfall: chaos engineering without observability is dangerous — if you cannot see what's breaking, the experiment just causes outages. Start small (single instance), monitor everything, and have a kill switch.
**Visual:**
```
Production cluster
   |
   v
[Chaos Monkey: kill 1 instance]
   |
   v
[Observability dashboard: did traffic stay healthy?]
   |              |
  yes            no
   |              |
   v              v
system is FT    find root cause + fix
```

### Q7. What is split-brain, and how do distributed systems prevent it?
**Answer:** Split-brain occurs when a network partition causes two subsets of nodes to each believe the other is dead, and both elect themselves as the active leader. Both then accept writes, producing divergent state that cannot be reconciled without data loss. It is one of the most dangerous failure modes in distributed systems. Prevention mechanisms: (1) Quorum-based leader election — a leader must be elected by a majority of nodes (Paxos, Raft); in a partition, only the majority side can elect a leader, and the minority side cannot. (2) Fencing tokens — each new leader gets an incrementing epoch number; storage systems reject writes from leaders with stale epochs, preventing the old leader from corrupting state after recovery. (3) Witness or quorum nodes — a small third site acts as a tiebreaker; in a 2-datacenter partition, the side that wins the witness becomes active. (4) STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) — the new leader forcibly powers off the old leader to prevent it from writing. Redis Sentinel, ZooKeeper, etcd, and CockroachDB all use quorum-based approaches. The pitfall: asynchronous replication without quorum (old MySQL/Postgres setups) is vulnerable to split-brain and can lose data on partition healing.
**Visual:**
```
Network partition:
  Site A: thinks B is dead -> elects itself leader
  Site B: thinks A is dead -> elects itself leader
  -> SPLIT BRAIN: both write, divergent state

Fix: Paxos quorum (3 sites, need 2 to agree)
  Site A: 1 vote (alone) -> cannot elect leader
  Site B+C: 2 votes -> elect leader (B becomes leader)
  Site A stays read-only until partition heals
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your microservice has 5 downstream dependencies. One of them, the recommendations service, becomes slow (5s response time). Without intervention, your service soon becomes unresponsive. What happened, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** This is a classic cascading failure. Your service calls the recommendations service synchronously; with 5s response times, each call holds a thread for 5s. If your thread pool has 200 threads and you receive 50 requests/second, after 4 seconds all 200 threads are blocked on recommendations, and your service stops responding to any request — even ones that don't need recommendations. Immediate mitigation: (1) Add a circuit breaker around the recommendations call with a 500ms timeout and a fallback to cached recommendations or omit them. This frees threads immediately when the downstream is slow. (2) Use bulkhead isolation — a dedicated thread pool for recommendations calls so its slowness cannot starve calls to other downstreams. (3) Reduce the timeout from 5s to 500ms — a slow response is usually worse than a fast error because it ties up resources. (4) Add backpressure: reject new requests with 503 when the thread pool is 80% full, rather than queuing indefinitely. Long-term: implement graceful degradation in the application code — every downstream call should have a documented fallback. Run chaos experiments that inject 5s latency into each downstream to verify the system survives. The lesson: synchronous downstream calls are the most common cause of cascading failures, and every one needs a timeout, circuit breaker, and fallback.
**Visual:**
```
Without protection:                With bulkhead + breaker:
  [shared pool: 200]                 [rec pool: 50]  [other: 150]
  rec slow (5s)                      rec slow (5s)
  -> 200 threads blocked in 4s       -> 50 blocked, breaker opens
  -> service dead                    -> other 150 healthy, serving
                                     -> rec falls back to cache
```

### Q2. You run a 100-node Cassandra cluster. One node starts OOMing every 10 minutes, causing its heartbeats to fail and triggering constant token-range ownership changes. What's the root cause, and how do you stabilize?
**Answer:** The OOM causes heartbeats to stop, which makes other nodes mark it as dead, triggering range ownership handoff to its replicas. When it recovers (after GC or restart), it rejoins and ownership shifts back. This thrashing causes high read-repair traffic, increased latency, and stress on the surviving nodes. Root causes to investigate: (1) The OOM itself — likely a memory leak in the JVM, an oversized row cache, or a compaction backlog filling the heap. Pull heap dumps and look at the dominator tree. (2) Compaction strategy — if the node is behind on compaction, SSTables pile up and read amplification causes extra memory pressure. Switch to LeveledCompactionStrategy or tune compaction throughput. (3) A hot partition — if one partition is being read heavily, the row cache may balloon; investigate the access pattern. Immediate stabilization: (1) Take the problem node out of rotation — decommission it or stop Cassandra so the cluster can stabilize without ownership thrashing. (2) Increase heap size if it was undersized, or add JEMALLOC to avoid native memory fragmentation. (3) Enable GC logging and identify the GC pause pattern. (4) Once the node is stable, re-add it during a low-traffic window with `nodetool rebuild` so it catches up without disrupting the cluster. The lesson: a single misbehaving node can destabilize the whole cluster; isolate it before debugging.
**Visual:**
```
Node-X: OOM -> heartbeat timeout -> marked dead
   -> replicas take over token ranges
Node-X: GC recovers -> rejoins -> ranges return
   -> repair traffic spikes
   -> next OOM -> repeat
Fix: decommission Node-X, debug OOM in isolation, re-add when stable
```

### Q3. You're designing a multi-region active-active service. The database team says they cannot achieve multi-region sync writes without 100ms latency. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** Multi-region active-active with synchronous writes is fundamentally bounded by the speed of light — you cannot make a write wait for consensus across continents in under ~50ms round-trip. The right answer is to not pretend otherwise and design around the constraint. Options: (1) Accept 100ms write latency for the workloads that need strong consistency (configuration, billing, identity) and use a regional primary for them. (2) Use eventual consistency for workloads that can tolerate it (user profiles, social posts, content metadata) — writes are fast in the local region and replicate async to other regions; conflicts resolved by last-write-wins or CRDTs. (3) Geo-partition the data so each user's writes go to their home region — for a global service, ~95% of writes can be local this way. (4) Use a globally consistent system like Spanner or CockroachDB only for the small subset of data that truly needs it, accepting the latency for those writes. (5) For the latency-critical path (e.g., real-time chat), use a regional primary with async cross-region replication for disaster recovery, accepting that a regional failure will cause a brief outage but not data loss beyond the replication window. The key principle: be honest about latency, partition the workload by consistency need, and don't force one consistency model on everything.
**Visual:**
```
Workload                  Consistency        Mechanism
Billing, identity         strong             Spanner (accepts 100ms)
User posts                eventual           regional RF=3 + async CRR
Real-time chat            strong, regional   regional primary + async DR
Notifications             eventual           regional queue + async fanout
```

### Q4. Your team's Kubernetes cluster has 100 nodes. The kube-apiserver becomes briefly unresponsive for 30 seconds, and many pods across different nodes restart simultaneously. Why, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** This is a control-plane dependency failure. Kubernetes pods are managed by kubelet on each node, which periodically reports pod status to the apiserver. If the apiserver is unreachable, kubelet cannot report status, and the control plane (controller-manager) may mark pods as unknown. Depending on the eviction policy and liveness probe configuration, this can cause pods to be restarted or evicted. Compounding factors: (1) Liveness probes that depend on the apiserver (e.g., checking a configmap) will fail, causing kubelet to restart the pod. (2) Deployments with rolling-update strategies may pause or roll back. (3) HorizontalPodAutoscaler cannot fetch metrics, freezing scaling decisions. Prevention: (1) Make liveness probes self-contained — they should check the pod's own health (HTTP /health endpoint), not depend on the apiserver. (2) Run a highly available apiserver (3+ replicas across AZs) — this is standard in managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) but easy to get wrong in self-hosted. (3) Tune `--pod-eviction-timeout` (default 5m) so transient apiserver blips don't trigger evictions. (4) Use PodDisruptionBudgets to limit voluntary disruptions. (5) Monitor the apiserver separately and alert on its latency. The lesson: the control plane is a shared dependency for every pod, and a brief apiserver blip can cascade to application-level restarts if probes are misconfigured.
**Visual:**
```
apiserver 30s blip
   |
   v
kubelets can't report status
   |
   v
pods marked Unknown
   |
   v
liveness probes that hit apiserver fail
   |
   v
kubelet restarts pods
Fix: self-contained probes + HA apiserver + longer eviction timeout
```

### Q5. A new microservice you've deployed is intermittently slow. Investigation shows GC pauses of 5-10 seconds every few minutes in the JVM. What patterns do you apply to make the service fault-tolerant despite this?
**Answer:** JVM GC pauses are a common cause of latency spikes and false-failure detections. The patterns to apply, in priority order: (1) Fix the GC itself — for a latency-sensitive service, switch to G1GC or ZGC with tuned pause targets (e.g., `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`). For most services, ZGC provides sub-10ms pauses. Investigate heap sizing — a heap that's too small triggers frequent GCs; too large triggers long full GCs. (2) Tune failure detector timeouts so a 10s GC pause does not cause the node to be marked dead — set heartbeat timeout above the worst-case GC pause plus margin. (3) Run multiple replicas behind a load balancer so a single node's GC pause is masked — the LB retries the request on a healthy node. (4) Use retries with jitter at the client so a single failed request is retried on another replica without user-visible impact. (5) Implement circuit breakers and bulkheads so a slow node does not cascade. (6) Long-term: investigate the memory allocation pattern that's causing GC pressure — often fixable by reducing object allocation in hot paths or switching to off-heap storage for caches. The principle: GC pauses are not rare events; design assuming they will happen, with redundancy and timeouts that absorb them.
**Visual:**
```
Node A: GC 10s pause
   |
   v
heartbeat timeout -> if timeout > 10s, no false-positive
   |
   v
LB retries on Node B -> user sees nothing
   |
   v
Node A resumes -> traffic resumes
Long-term: ZGC, smaller heap, less allocation
```

### Q6. Your payment service uses synchronous replication across two AZs. A network partition between the AZs causes writes to fail entirely for 30 seconds. How do you make this fault-tolerant?
**Answer:** The partition breaks the synchronous replication path: the primary cannot reach the secondary, so it cannot satisfy the "wait for both" requirement, and writes fail. This is the classic CAP-theorem availability trade-off of strong consistency — a partition forces a choice between consistency (block writes) and availability (accept writes that may diverge). The fix depends on the workload's priorities: (1) For the payment service where data integrity is paramount, accept the brief outage — better to fail writes than to risk double-spending or inconsistent state. Add retries with backoff at the client and queue writes for later processing if needed. (2) Add a third AZ (or a witness site) and use Paxos/Raft quorum — with 3 replicas, a partition that isolates one AZ leaves the other two as a quorum that can continue writes. (3) Use a "available during partition" mode for non-critical writes — e.g., accept the write locally with a flag, and reconcile after the partition heals. (4) Add a standby cluster in a third region with async replication so a complete AZ-pair failure doesn't take the service down. (5) Make the partition visible — alert on replication lag and write failures so the team knows immediately. The key principle: for a payment system, you should accept brief unavailability over inconsistency, and design the client to retry gracefully. Multi-AZ quorum is the standard architecture.
**Visual:**
```
2 AZs (partition-tolerant fail):
  AZ-A primary <-> AZ-B sync replica
  partition -> primary can't reach replica -> writes FAIL

3 AZs (partition-tolerant continue):
  AZ-A <-> AZ-B <-> AZ-C  (Paxos)
  partition A | B+C -> B+C form quorum -> writes continue
```

### Q7. You are designing a global notification service that must continue working if a region fails. Walk through the architecture and the failure modes you defend against.
**Answer:** Architecture: (1) Deploy the service in 3+ regions (us-east, eu-west, ap-southeast) with active-active traffic — each region serves its local users and can serve any user if another region fails. (2) Use a multi-region database with async replication (DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra multi-DC, Spanner) so writes in each region propagate to the others within seconds. (3) Use a global load balancer (Route 53, Cloudflare, Anycast) that routes users to the nearest healthy region and fails over within seconds when a region is marked unhealthy. (4) Each region has its own queue (Kafka or SQS) for async processing; consumers in each region can drain the queue of a failed region via cross-region queue replication. (5) Use idempotency keys so duplicate notifications (from retries or failover) are deduplicated. Failure modes defended against: AZ failure (multi-AZ deployment in each region), region failure (traffic fails over to other regions), network partition (queue replication reconciles eventually), individual service crash (multiple replicas per service), database failure (multi-region replication with automated failover). Failure modes not fully defended: simultaneous multi-region failure (extremely rare; requires offline backups and DR plan), split-brain during partition (mitigated by quorum-based leader election), and consistency violations during failover (mitigated by idempotency and last-write-wins or CRDT conflict resolution). The architecture is expensive but justified for a service where downtime means missed 2FA codes or missed appointment reminders.
**Visual:**
```
        [Global DNS / Anycast LB]
        /         |           \
   [us-east]  [eu-west]  [ap-southeast]
      |          |           |
      +--- DynamoDB Global Tables (async replication) ---+
      |          |           |
   [Kafka]    [Kafka]     [Kafka]   (cross-region replication)
      |          |           |
   [workers] [workers]   [workers]

Region fails -> DNS fails over in 30s -> other regions absorb load
               -> queues replicate, no notification lost (idempotent)
```
